teaser: Moscow told him his art was too much about feelings. His answer, five years on: forty circles.
review_notes:
Kandinsky's program for the Moscow Institute of Artistic Culture (INKhUK) was rejected by his colleagues in 1920; he left Russia in December 1921.
Painted January to February 1926 in Dessau. Size about 140 x 140 cm.
His remarks on the circle (synthesis of the greatest oppositions) come from a 1930 letter to Will Grohmann; paraphrased here, not quoted.
Guggenheim visited the Dessau studio in 1930 with Hilla Rebay; the museum holds more than 150 Kandinsky works.
57 works confiscated from German museums in 1937.
The count of 'about forty' circles is approximate.

lesson.text: In 1920, Wassily Kandinsky wrote a teaching program for a new art institute in Moscow. His colleagues voted it down. Too personal, they said, too interested in what a color makes you feel. The young revolutionary artists wanted rulers, engineering and useful objects, and he was 54 and out of step.

He left Russia the next year and never went back. Germany took him in, first in Weimar, then in Dessau, where he taught at the Bauhaus school of art and design. There, in the first weeks of 1926, he painted a square canvas using a single shape repeated about forty times.
Kandinsky limited himself to circles to prove a point his Moscow critics had missed: the strictest geometry can still be full of feeling.
Each circle here behaves differently. Some are solid, some see-through, some wear a glowing rim. Before going further, hunt for the one that seems to be looking back at you.
One pale circle on the left holds a black dot, like the pupil of an eye. Where is it?

spots.title: The eye
spots.text: A lilac disc, a double dark outline, and a black dot pushed off-center. Because the dot is not in the middle, the circle seems to glance up and to the right, toward the big blue one.

lesson.text: That little trick tells you how the whole picture works. Nothing is drawn except circles, yet you read glances, weights and distances. A big dark disc feels heavy. A small yellow one feels far away or light. Your mind supplies the drama.

In Dessau, Kandinsky lived in one half of a two-family house designed for Bauhaus teachers. The other half belonged to his friend, the painter Paul Klee. The two shared a garden and took tea together.

For Kandinsky the circle held opposites together. It is the calmest of shapes and also the most unstable, since it has no top, no bottom and could roll away. He said it pointed, more than any other form, toward something beyond the visible world.
He was not illustrating astronomy. Still, the layout he chose feels like a system of planets, with one giant body and a crowd of satellites.

lesson.title: A small universe
lesson.text: Travel from the center outward, the way the painting pulls your eye.

spots.title: Eclipse
spots.text: A black disc sits off-center inside a blue one, leaving a blue crescent. A fuzzy white halo surrounds both, like the glow around the sun during an eclipse.

spots.title: Overlaps
spots.text: Where circles cross, Kandinsky paints a third color: yellow over blue goes olive, pink over ochre goes orange. They look like sheets of tinted glass, though it is all opaque oil paint.

spots.title: Green ring
spots.text: A green disc with a small black center ringed in pale blue. It touches the big blue circle at one point only, like a moon just about to break away.

spots.title: Pale planet
spots.text: Far from the center, a large lilac circle gathers its own companions: turquoise, tan, a red dot and a black dot. A second, quieter system.

lesson.text: Notice the background too. It is not flat black. Kandinsky brushed it in cloudy grays and blue-greens, with darker pools around many of the circles, so each one seems to float in its own pocket of space.

When the Nazis came to power, the Bauhaus was closed and Kandinsky moved to France. In 1937, German authorities removed 57 of his works from the country's museums as “degenerate,” their word for modern art they wanted to ridicule.

By then an American had already taken his side. The mining magnate Solomon Guggenheim visited Kandinsky's Dessau studio in 1930 and kept buying for years. This painting went to New York, to the museum that carries the collector's name.
So the artist rejected in Moscow ended up at the heart of a museum on Fifth Avenue. And the building itself, opened in 1959, is a white spiral: a ramp of circles, turning one above the other.

The Guggenheim Museum owns more than 150 works by Kandinsky, one of the largest holdings anywhere. Its first director, Hilla Rebay, called this kind of art “non-objective,” meaning painting that shows no object at all.

quiz.question: Why did Kandinsky's Moscow colleagues reject his teaching program in 1920?
options: They found it too personal and focused on feeling
They thought it was too technical
They disliked his use of circles
quiz.explanation: They wanted engineering and useful objects, not the study of what colors make you feel.

quiz.question: What happens where two circles overlap in this painting?
options: The top one hides the other completely
The overlap is left as bare canvas
quiz.explanation: Kandinsky paints the overlap in a blended color, as if the circles were tinted glass.

quiz.question: Who shared a two-family house with Kandinsky in Dessau?
quiz.explanation: Kandinsky and Paul Klee lived in the two halves of the same teachers' house.

quiz.question: What does the big blue circle with its black disc and white halo resemble?
quiz.explanation: The off-center black disc and the white glow recall the sun during an eclipse.

quiz.question: What did the term “non-objective” mean for the Guggenheim's first director?
options: Painting that shows no object at all
quiz.explanation: Hilla Rebay used it for painting that depicts no object.

facts.text: The background of Several Circles is a perfectly flat, even black.
facts.explanation: It is brushed in cloudy grays and blue-greens, with darker pools around the circles.

facts.text: Kandinsky left Russia in the early 1920s and never returned.
facts.explanation: After his program was rejected he left the next year and settled in Germany, then France.

facts.text: The Nazis celebrated Kandinsky's paintings and added them to German museums.
facts.explanation: In 1937 they removed 57 of his works from German museums as “degenerate.”
